candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Deuteronomy
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 25:1-19. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. 1 Cor 9:9, 1 Tim 5:18.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Deuteronomy (c. 365 AD)

On 'Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn' (Deu 25:4), Ephrem reads the agricultural-mercy statute as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of Paul's argument for ministerial support: cited at 1 Cor 9:9 and 1 Tim 5:18 with the gloss 'Doth God take care for oxen? or saith he it altogether for our sakes? For our sakes, no doubt, this is written.' The verse becomes the apostolic warrant for the priest's right to be sustained by the eucharistic offerings of the people. Tewahedo canonical-economy cites Deu 25:4 + 1 Cor 9:9 as the canonical doubled-witness for the lay-support of the priest and the monastery — the worker is worthy of his hire.

On 'Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn' (Deu 25:4), Ephrem reads the agricultural-mercy statute as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of Paul's argument for ministerial support: cited at 1 Cor 9:9 and 1 Tim 5:18 with the gloss 'Doth God take care for oxen? or saith he it altogether for our sakes? For our sakes, no doubt, this is written.' The verse becomes the apostolic warrant for the priest's right to be sustained by the eucharistic offerings of the people. Tewahedo canonical-economy cites Deu 25:4 + 1 Cor 9:9 as the canonical doubled-witness for the lay-support of the priest and the monastery — the worker is worthy of his hire.
